title: Bellman Ford Algorithm
problemStatement: Single-source shortest paths on a weighted directed graph that may contain negative edge weights. Also detect whether a negative-weight cycle is reachable from the source. (Dijkstra fails here and can loop forever on negative cycles.)
intuition: A simple path has ≤ V−1 edges (V edges ⇒ a repeated vertex ⇒ a cycle). Without negative cycles we never need cycles on a shortest path, so relax all edges V−1 times and every shortest simple path can fully propagate. One more improving pass ⇒ reachable negative cycle. Works with negative weights; Dijkstra does not — BF is the correct algorithm for negatives / cycle detect, not a “brute Dijkstra.”

approaches.title: Trap: Dijkstra on negatives
approaches.idea: Dijkstra assumes once a node is settled at min cost, it is final. Negative edges break that; a negative cycle can make distances decrease forever. Use Bellman-Ford instead.
approaches.code:
# Do NOT use Dijkstra when negative weights (or neg-cycle detect) exist.
# Dijkstra → wrong answers / non-termination on negative cycles.

approaches.title: Optimal: Bellman-Ford (+ nth pass for cycle)
approaches.idea: dist[src]=0, others ∞. Relax all edges n−1 times. Then one more pass: if any edge still improves → negative cycle (return e.g. [-1]). Skip relaxations from unreachable u (dist[u]=∞).
algorithm: Build edge list of (u, v, w) on a directed graph
For iter = 1 … n−1: for each edge (u,v,w), if dist[u] + w < dist[v] → dist[v] = dist[u] + w
Nth pass: if any edge still relaxes → negative cycle reachable from src
approaches.whyWorks: V vertices + ≥ V edges on a path ⇒ some vertex repeats ⇒ a cycle. Shortest paths (no neg-cycle) are simple ⇒ ≤ V−1 edges ⇒ V−1 full relax passes suffice. A further improve means the improving “path” has a cycle whose total weight is < 0.
approaches.dryRun:
Propagation along a chain (worst case needs V−1 passes):

    0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4     (4 edges, V=5 ⇒ V−1 = 4)

    Pass 1: 0 → 1
    Pass 2: 0 → 1 → 2
    Pass 3: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3
    Pass 4: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4

Edge order can let several hops update in one pass — V−1 is the guarantee, not “exactly one new edge each time.”

Numeric example, src=0, n=4:

         4
    0 ───────→ 1
    │          │
   5│         -3
    │          │
    ↓    2     ↓
    2 ───────→ 3

Edges: (0,1,4) (0,2,5) (1,3,-3) (2,3,2)

Init:     dist = [0, ∞, ∞, ∞]
Round 1:  → [0, 4, 5, 1]
Rounds 2–3: no further improves
Nth pass: no improve → no neg-cycle
Answer: [0, 4, 5, 1]

If a reachable cycle still improves on the nth pass → return [-1].
limitations: Slower than Dijkstra when all weights ≥ 0 — still choose BF when negatives / cycle detect matter
Works on directed graphs; undirected needs conversion (see notes)

python.notes: Edge list (u,v,w). Guard dist[u] != INF so ∞+w never “updates.” Return [-1] (or None) on neg-cycle.

java.notes: Same n−1 + nth pass. null ⇒ cycle.

cpp.notes: Empty return = neg-cycle. Use long long for negative weights.

specialTechnique.title: Why V−1 iterations, what one pass means, nth-pass cycle detect
specialTechnique.body:
1) Why V − 1 iterations?

   A simple path can contain at most V − 1 edges.

   Why? If a path visits V vertices and uses V or more edges, some vertex must repeat → that is a cycle.

   For shortest paths without negative cycles we never need a cycle: removing a non-negative cycle cannot make the path worse. So the shortest path is a simple path with at most V−1 edges.

   ⇒ Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V−1 times.

2) What does one iteration actually mean?

   Important intuition — information propagates along the path:

       0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4

   Shortest path 0→4 uses 4 edges (V=5 ⇒ need up to 4 passes):

       Pass 1: 0 → 1
       Pass 2: 0 → 1 → 2
       Pass 3: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3
       Pass 4: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4

   After at most V−1 passes, every shortest simple path has had enough opportunities to propagate.

   Caveat: not necessarily exactly one new edge per iteration — edge ordering can let several vertices update in a single pass. V−1 is a worst-case guarantee.

3) Why does one extra pass detect a negative cycle?

   After V−1 complete relaxation passes, if there is no reachable negative cycle, distances are already optimal.

   One more pass:

       for u, v, w in edges:
           if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
               return [-1]

   If something can still become smaller, the improving walk must use ≥ V edges ⇒ it contains a cycle. Because traversing that cycle made the cost smaller, that cycle’s total weight is < 0.

   ⇒ reachable negative cycle.

——— Extra notes ———

4) Undirected → directed
   u ——w—— v  ⇒  u→v (w) and v→u (w).
   ⚠ If w < 0, those two edges form a neg-cycle of weight 2w.

5) Negative-cycle sketch

         -2
    1 ────────→ 2
    ↑           │
   +2│          │ -1
    │           ↓
    └────────── 3

   −2 + (−1) + 2 = −1 < 0.

6) Complexity
   BF O(V·E) vs Dijkstra O((V+E) log V). Choose BF for negatives / cycle detect.

7) Interview: “at most k edges” ⇒ only k BF rounds (cheapest flights within k stops).

whyWorks:
1) V−1: path with ≥ V edges repeats a vertex (cycle). No neg-cycle ⇒ shortest path is simple ⇒ ≤ V−1 edges ⇒ V−1 relax rounds suffice.

2) One pass: each full scan of all edges can push the shortest-path “frontier” one hop further along a chain (0→1, then →2, …). Edge order may advance several hops in one pass; V−1 is the guarantee.

3) Extra pass: any improve after V−1 means the walk has a cycle and that cycle lowered cost ⇒ total cycle weight < 0 (reachable neg-cycle).
edgeCases: Negative cycle reachable from src → report cycle (don’t return finite dist)
Negative edges but no cycle → valid shortest paths
Undirected graph with a negative edge → conversion creates a neg-cycle
commonMistakes: Calling Bellman-Ford the “brute force” for Dijkstra
Skipping the nth pass (miss negative cycles)
Relaxing when dist[u] is ∞ (∞ + w garbage)
Forgetting undirected → two directed edges (and the neg-edge trap)
patternRecognition: Detect negative cycle in a weighted digraph
“At most k edges” → BF with k rounds (e.g. cheapest flights)
followUps: Cheapest flights within k stops — only k+1 rounds?
interviewInsight: Say three things: (1) simple path ≤ V−1 edges else a vertex repeats; (2) each pass can extend the path by one hop along 0→1→2→… so V−1 passes suffice; (3) one more improve ⇒ cycle with weight < 0. Then contrast Dijkstra.
